title: Collision problem: Theta(N^(1/2)) classical queries vs Theta(N^(1/3)) quantum queries (Brassard-Hoyer-Tapp)
problem_statement: Given oracle access to a 2-to-1 function f on N = 2^n points (every value in the image has exactly two preimages), output a collision: two distinct inputs a, b with f(a) = f(b).

input.parameter: n = number of input bits; N = 2^n domain points.
input.size_measure: Query model: cost is the number of oracle calls. The harness materialises the N-entry table (a uniformly random 2-to-1 function with values in {0, ..., 2N - 1}) only so that the oracle can be simulated.

algorithms.name: classical birthday search
algorithms.idea: Query distinct points in uniformly random order until a value repeats.
algorithms.pseudocode: for x in random permutation: if f(x) seen at x': return {x', x}
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(sqrt N) = Theta(2^(n/2)) queries expected: E[Q] = sum_q prod_{i=1}^{q-1} (N-2i)/(N-i) ~ sqrt(pi N / 2); at most N/2 + 1
algorithms.correctness: A repeated value is a collision by definition; by pigeonhole one appears within N/2 + 1 queries.

algorithms.name: Brassard-Hoyer-Tapp, known number of marked points
algorithms.idea: Query a set K of k = N^(1/3) points classically; if K contains no collision, exactly k other points are partners of points in K, and Grover search with this known count finds one in about (pi/4) sqrt(N/k) iterations.
algorithms.pseudocode: see implementation (BHT 1998, algorithm Collision(F, k) with k = N^(1/3), K = {0..k-1})
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(N^(1/3)) = Theta(2^(n/3)) queries expected: k + (2m + 1)/sin^2((2m+1) theta) with sin^2 theta = k/N, m = floor(pi/(4 theta)), counting 2 queries per Grover iteration; about 2.57 N^(1/3)
algorithms.space_complexity: n qubits plus a table of k classical values readable in superposition (BHT: Theta(N^(1/3)) space)
algorithms.correctness: Brassard, Hoyer & Tapp (arXiv note 1997, Theorem 1; conference version LATIN '98): O(k + sqrt(N/k)) expected evaluations, O(N^(1/3)) for k = N^(1/3). Each candidate is checked classically, so the output is always a correct collision (Las Vegas).

algorithms.name: Brassard-Hoyer-Tapp with BBHT exponential search (unknown number of marked points)
algorithms.idea: As above, but K is random and the Grover search does not use the number of marked points: BBHT exponential search (random iteration counts below a growing bound m, m <- 6m/5). BHT prescribe this version for functions that are not exactly r-to-1.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(N^(1/3)) queries expected (BBHT Theorem 3: O(sqrt(N/t)) iterations for t marked items); exact expectation about 3.9 N^(1/3) for large N, reached only for n >~ 18
algorithms.correctness: BHT (arXiv note 1997, section 2, general case) with BBHT 1998 Theorem 3. Las Vegas.

lower_bounds.bound: Omega(sqrt N) = Omega(2^(n/2)) queries for bounded error
lower_bounds.source: Birthday argument: on a uniformly random 2-to-1 function, after i collision-free queries ANY next query completes a pair with probability exactly i/(N-i), so q queries reveal a collision with probability at most q^2/(2(N-q)), and guessing an unseen pair succeeds with probability at most 1/(N-q-1); Yao's principle gives the randomized bound. Stated as the classical optimum (expected Theta(sqrt N)) in the arXiv note of Brassard, Hoyer & Tapp (1997). It also follows from the classical lower bound for Simon's problem (simon-classical-vs-quantum), because every Simon instance is 2-to-1 and any collision reveals s.

lower_bounds.bound: N/2 + 1 queries in the worst case for algorithms that are always correct (N >= 4)
lower_bounds.source: Elementary adversary argument: answer the first N/2 queries with distinct values; every unqueried point can still be the partner of every queried one, so no pair is certain. Pigeonhole makes N/2 + 1 sufficient.

lower_bounds.bound: Omega(N^(1/3)) = Omega(2^(n/3)) queries for bounded error (BHT is optimal up to a constant factor)
lower_bounds.setting: query (oracle) model, unconditional; proven for the decision version (1-to-1 vs 2-to-1), which the search version solves with one extra check
lower_bounds.source: Aaronson & Shi 2004 (proof requires a codomain of size at least 3N/2, which this harness's codomain of size 2N satisfies; as stated by Kutin 2005); Kutin 2005 and Ambainis 2005 remove the range condition

relationship: Proven POLYNOMIAL separation in the query model, tight on both sides: Theta(N^(1/2)) classical (randomized) vs Theta(N^(1/3)) quantum. Relation to Simon's problem: Simon's functions are exactly the 2-to-1 functions whose pairs are the cosets {x, x XOR s}, and on them finding a collision is equivalent to finding s (s = a XOR b; conversely {0, s} is a collision), as the arXiv note of Brassard, Hoyer & Tapp remarks. With that XOR structure, O(n) = O(log N) quantum queries suffice (Simon), an exponential speedup; without it the quantum query complexity is Theta(N^(1/3)), only a polynomial speedup. Classically both problems take Theta(sqrt N). The structure, not the 2-to-1 promise, is what makes the speedup exponential.

verification.method: V1: every output of all three algorithms is checked against the instance (distinct indices, equal values) on random 2-to-1 functions for n = 1..14 (quantum versions simulated exactly with lib/qsim.py and lib/qsearch.py up to n = 12). The problem is a relation (N/2 valid answers), so harness.equal does not require the implementations to return the same collision; correctness rests on the independent check. V2 measures QUERY COUNTS reported through lib.qsim.Oracle, averaged over random instances; every Grover iteration is charged 2 queries (compute and uncompute). Sample sizes (100 / 40 / 100 instances per n) were chosen so that the standard error of the fitted alpha predicted from the per-n spread is 0.012 / 0.013 / 0.022. The exact expectations give alpha = 0.997 (classical vs 2^(n/2)), 1.027 (BHT, known count, vs 2^(n/3)) and 1.154 (BHT with exponential search, vs 2^(n/3)); the last is pre-asymptotic: E(n)/N^(1/3) rises from 2.50 at n = 3 to 3.75 at n = 15 and settles at 3.90 near n = 27, and the exact slope over n = 15..30 is 1.009. experiments/2026-10-07_collision_expected_queries.py compares simulated means with these exact expectations: after correcting the first version of bht.py (see research/2026-10-07_quantum_entries.md), all 17 z-scores have |z| <= 2.12 except classical n = 8 (z = +3.19), which a follow-up with 200000 fresh instances and an independent 10^6-sample sampler resolved as chance (z = +0.46 and -0.95).

caveats: A separation relative to an oracle, and only polynomial (exponent 1/2 vs 1/3); it does not imply BQP != BPP. Query accounting charges 2 queries per Grover iteration because the marking depends on the value f(x), which must be computed and uncomputed; BHT's proof counts one evaluation of f per evaluation of the marking function, so their constant is smaller, but the exponent 1/3 is unchanged. BHT's quantum algorithm needs Theta(N^(1/3)) classical values to be readable in superposition (a quantum-readable memory), which BHT themselves flag as a practical resource issue. The quantum algorithms are Las Vegas (always correct, random query count), so V2 fits expected counts. The fitted slope of the exponential-search variant over n = 3..15 is pre-asymptotic (exact value 1.154); see verification. In the measured range (n = 3..15) the BBHT variant is pre-asymptotic: its counts would also fit the classical 2^(n/2) (alpha 0.776 against it, inside the 0.25 band; deviation analysis F3), so it is NOT given that rival and does not by itself demonstrate the separation there. The separation is demonstrated by the known-t variant, whose counts reject 2^(n/2) as a declared rival (RL-056).
notes: Completes the 2-to-1 family in the dataset: Simon's problem (2-to-1 with XOR structure: exponential quantum speedup) vs the collision problem (2-to-1 without structure: polynomial speedup, Theta(N^(1/3)), proven optimal). The quantum lower bound also implies Omega(N^(2/3)) for element distinctness (see staging/element-distinctness-quantum-walk).
